titleStmt.title: Stress and the Waw 'Consecutive' in Biblical Hebrew

analytic.title: Stress and the Waw 'Consecutive' in Biblical Hebrew

monogr.title: Journal of the American Oriental Society

docTitle.titlePart: STRESS AND THE WAW “CONSECUTIVE” IN BIBLICAL HEBREW

body.p: The stress patterns of biblical Hebrew are most easily explained as derived from a stage in which words ending in a consonant had final stress, words ending in a vowel, penultimate. Consequently, stress position in the great majority of verb forms with waw consecutive—perfect and imperfect—must have been the same, at this stage, as in the corresponding forms in other uses, and in most cases the forms would have been identical. Suggestions are made as to how the marks now distinguishing waw consecutive forms arose, and as to the historical context in which such marks became necessary.

list.item: 1. THE NATURE AND ORIGIN OF waw CONSECUTIVE FORMS IN HEBREW are a perennial problem. Attempts to find a solution always involve stress patterns, but these are invariably regarded as the result of a historical process, not as part of an existing system. Consequently a part of the information which they convey is ignored.

body.p: 2. The stress patterns of biblical Hebrew can be described as follows:
2.1 A word ending in a consonant has final stress, as dā'ḇār, daḇā'rîm, qā'ṭal, qəṭal'tem , yiq'ṭōl, wayyiq'ṭōlūn.
EXCEPT (i) Segolate form nouns and corresponding structures, as ke'sep , se'per, mamle'ket, ḥe'rep , wayyi'ben, bəna'yik .
(ii) Some waw consecutive imperfect forms with open penultimate syllable (as described in #10.1), also hiššā'mēr (see note 19), in contextual position.
(iii) 3fs perfect verb forms with 2fs or 3mpl suffix, as gənāḇā'tam (Gen 31:32), šōḇā'ḇtek (Is 47:10).

2.2 A word ending in a vowel has final stress if it derives from a root III ʾ, or (except for the forms mentioned in #2.3) III h, as gālô', yiglô', wayyeš'e', gālû', rā'ê, bārā', nāśā', or where the final vowel represents a suffixed pronoun, the fs nominal ending, or the “gentilic” ending, or a similar ending in a few other nouns, as dəḇārô' , dəḇārî', šānā', ʿazzā'tî, napta'lî.

2.3 A word ending in a vowel also has final stress in (other) forms ending in -CāCV. These occur in contextual position only. Examples are verb forms ending in a vowel representing a pronominal element, as qāṭā'lû, tiqṭə'lû, yiqṭə'lû, and some words from root III h: nouns of the form pərî', ḥŏlî', and the corresponding verb forms as yaḥ'î, yah'î, also some pronominal morphs, as ʾănî', hinnənî' , dəḇārakā'.
EXCEPT forms in which -āh “directional” is bound to a noun originally ending -CVCC, as ʾō'hĕlā also lā'yəlā.
body.note: ¹ This is true even of the description of syllable structure and stress patterns in J. Blau, “Hebrew Stress Shifts, Pretonic Lengthening, and Segolization: Possible Cases of Aramaic Interference in Hebrew Syllable Structure” in Israel Oriental Studies 8 (1978), 91–106 (henceforward “Blau”). This description is “mainly synchronic” (p. 92). The reason for the omission of construct forms (as having weak or no stress) is no doubt valid historically, but is not true of the primary evidence. Stress is marked here by a vertical stroke (') before the stressed vowel. The Hebrew vowels are represented as u (shureq, qibbus), o (holem), ɔ (qames), a (patah), ε (segol), e (sere), i (hireq), ə (shewa), ŏ, ă, ĕ, (composite shewa). A circumflex denotes the presence of a vowel letter, w for û, ô, y for î. Other non-consonantal uses of w, y, and h are ignored.

² In the cases described in #3, a word appears in a special pausal form at the end of a syntactic/semantic unit (pausal position). Within these units (contextual position) the contextual form is used. For the distribution of pausal forms, see JSS 25 (1980), 165–179, VT 31 (1981), 186–199, and note 5 below.
³ Both words are in pausal position. For similar forms in contextual position, see Jos 2:6, Is 47:14, Hos 2:14, Ps 48:7 and Rut 4:15.
